What are the 3 major classes of an IP network?

In a class A address, the first octet is the network portion, so the class A address of, 10.1.25.1, has a major network address of 10. Octets 2, 3, and 4 (the next 24 bits) are for the hosts. Class A addresses are used for networks that have more than 65,536 hosts (actually, up to 16,581,375 hosts!).

In a class B address, the first two octets are the network portion, so the class B address of, 172.16.122.204, has a major network address of 172.16. Octets 3 and 4 (the next 16 bits) are for the hosts. Class B addresses are used for networks that have between 256 and 65,536 hosts.

In a class C address, the first three octets are the network portion. The class C address of, 193.18.9.45, has a major network address of 193.18.9. Octet 4 (the last 8 bits) is for hosts. Class C addresses are used for networks with less than 254 hosts

Why do you do what you do?

I drift, which is to say I like to see something of the world

Hitchiking is my favorite way of transport since I never know where I will end up

For food: I restore houses, do somee carpenting if need be, I make and trade sculptures, sheer sheep, cut wood, almost anything which needs be done in echange for a place to sleep, a meal or some cash

Have you ever found yourself in a 'dangerous' situation whilst hitch-hiking?

Do you develop friendships with the people you meet during your travels?

Rarely: the most dangerous part for me is the weather, gotten into a few situations in which I began to show the first signs of hypothermia but nothing worse (touches wood)

Washed-away roads, once; other than that I try to watch my step, think ahead and plan on how to get from A to B, and NEVER get in a car if I have a bad vibe

Friendship: yes, a lot and very often: one friend drove about two hundred miles to pick me up when I got stranded around Christmas a couple of years ago and I had no possile way to stay where I was without taking the real possibility of dying through hypothermia

We're still good friends and I'm forever grateful for her friendship

With other people I have lasting friendships and drop by once in a while for a couple of days if I happen to be in the neighourhood
Thanks for the reply, kinda different to what I expected. Hope you stay warm and safe & good luck with your future travels :)

Less natural problems, more problems with individuals (i.e. facing problems like squatters would). I would have thought that friendships would have been more fleeting 'acquaintances' rather than lasting.

To be able to question a perspective that disproves my assumptions is always an interesting experience.

:p

There has been the occasional a-hole who doesn't like hitchhikers, but I shrug it off

Oh yes, many friendships are aquaintances as is only normal; fortunately, i've gotten to know so many people whom I consider as good friends and I do my best to keep in touch as much as possible (postcards or emails for birthdays, occasional emails to see how life's going there; tat sort of thing)

A lot of those people I've gotten to know on a deeper level: I've seen their childrn bein born (well, not literally) and grow up: it's awesome they see me as part of the family (encouraged by their parents I must add)
What do your monthly living expenses cost you on average? Are there certain geographic locations where people are generally more friendly and helpful?

Hmm, about 30 euros on food on average and a changing amount since I do occasionally smoke (price varies in different countries). That's about it; I've survived last winter on about 120 euros, which saw me through for about 4 months

Yes, there are certain regions where people are more open to hitchhikers either due to a general attitude or because the land forces you to stop for people (Scotland, Norway, EasternEurope wherethere might be 1 car passing in over an hour which almost always will stop)

Spain is terrible for hitchhiking, because people hardly stop for people they don't know. Same goes for most urban areas: people are either too busy, too afraid or just don't agree with this style of life. Which is sad for them but I avoid the large cities in general.

For helpfulness! countryside, the poorer the more helpful, strangely enough (or not :p).
When did you start being a full-time nomad? Was it a decision, or kind of just happened? What where some struggles starting?

Sorry for the long delay in reply: have been on the road again and just got back 3 days ago (2 of which this site was busy)

It was back in 2011, when I was coming out of a deep depression due to being unemployed for more than 2 years, stuck in a dead-end parttime job. I heard a phrase on the internet which I haven't forgotten (though I don't remember who said it) which went 'tell me why you think it's normal that you need to pay to be allowed to live on the planet you were born on?'

And then a penny dropped. I suddenly realized why I was depressed, suicidal and generally fed up with the world, the economic system and politics of everyday life. It was because I was being forced to play a game I never agreed to play; forced to play by rules not by my making nor consent. I thought about the logic of being 'forced' to work for 40 hours a week for a measly paycheck, to work for 40 years of my life with a daily rhythm which didn't seem to diverge from getting up around 7, having breakfast, getting to work from 9 to 5, getting back home, eating something, watching tv and repeating that for the next 40 years or so, without even the remotest possibility to get a pension, and being by then too old to do the things I would like to do. Besides, most of my salary was spent on just being allowed a place to sleep (read: rent), I did spend some money on books, rarely on clothing and never on gadgets. The idea of having to pay for food (most of which grows from seeds which, if planted in dirt, could sprout food all by themselves. Radical idea, right? I know :p)

So I started to think about what was really important to me: so far I have found 6 elements essential for me and my well-being:

-clean air -clean water -clean food (I plant vegetable seeds wherever I can, sometimes they take root, sometimes not) - good health -good friends - a place to sleep

Then I thought about my obligation to participate in a society which forces me to do things I do not like to do, forces me to consume, and makes me complicant to warcrimes by me participating in said political system. The question I asked was 'Am I obligated to, play this game? To obey these rules? No. The only rule I as a human being am obliged to follow is the Golden Rule (Do whatever you will, but do not harm others). So I quit my appartment, strapped on my backpack and left. 3 years later and I've seen things, met people, had an awesome time and-most important of all- haven't gone to bed on an empty stomach even once. :)

Thanks for taking out the time to write out all that, it's really impacted me. I appreciate it a lot. Can I ask you a few more questions? When you first started, what did you leave with ( / What supplies did you take?)? You would have met a lot of people and I was just wondering what you have noticed most about people? Also, on the subject of people, what was(has been(?)) the most amount of charity ever given to you whilst roaming around? Thanks once again :)

No worries, it's an AMA, right? :) I left with a backpack, tent, map, spair pants, 2 tshirts, 4 pairs of underwear (socks and boxers), walking shoes, small pan and peastrainer, toothpaste, toothbrush, hairbrush, first-aid kit, fishing-lines and -hooks, 2 whittling knives, some food, a poncho and a coat. And my lifesavings, which were about 700 euro's. That saw me through the most part of a year.

What I noticed most about people is this: - the bigger and more expensive the car is, the smaller the chances of getting a ride are. Most help or hospitality comes from those who have very little. - people are afraid in the metropolitan areas, so no good for hitching a ride. - a lot of people are acting like zombies, when they're distracted by tv, buying/consuming. Most of them have no idea in how deep a mess this planet is right now (talking economically, politically, environmentally etc) - people are getting really fed up with a political and economical system which has royally screwed them for the last 30 years but have no idea how to do anything better. Most are caught up in the 'trap' of marriage, children, mortgage, jobs. Talk about mounting the barricades and erecting the guillotines again has risen quite sharply the last couple of years - when you least expect it, there will be help coming; At least, that's how it has worked for me. Mostly part of the mindset: I got really stoic about finding work or food or a place to sleep but somehow I've always ended up somewhere good (knocks on wood). So far, so good :)

Most amount of charity: a practically complete new set of clothing, coming from an old ladies deceased husband (never worn, everything in my size)
